{{DISPLAYTITLE:Volume of an ''n''-ball}}
{{Short description|Size of a mathematical ball}}
[[File:Volumes of unit balls.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Volumes of balls in dimensions 0 through 25; unit ball in red.]]

In [[geometry]], a [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] is a region comprising all points within a fixed [[Metric space|distance]], called the [[radius]], from a given point; that is, it is the region enclosed by a [[sphere]] or [[hypersphere]]. An {{math|''n''}}-ball is a ball in an {{math|''n''}}-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. The '''volume of a {{math|''n''}}-ball''' is the [[Lebesgue measure]] of this ball, which generalizes to any dimension the usual volume of a ball in [[3-dimensional space]]. The volume of a {{mvar|n}}-ball of radius {{mvar|R}} is <math>R^nV_n,</math> where <math>V_n</math> is the volume of the [[unit ball|unit {{mvar|n}}-ball]], the {{mvar|n}}-ball of radius {{math|1}}.

The [[real number]] <math>V_n</math> can be expressed via a two-dimension [[recurrence relation]].
Closed-form expressions involve the [[gamma function|gamma]], [[factorial]], or [[double factorial]] function. 
The volume can also be expressed in terms of <math>A_n</math>, the [[area]] of the [[unit n-sphere|unit {{mvar|n}}-sphere]].

=== Closed form ===
The {{math|''n''}}-dimensional volume of a Euclidean ball of [[radius]] {{math|''R''}} in {{math|''n''}}-dimensional Euclidean space is:<ref>Equation 5.19.4, ''NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions.'' http://dlmf.nist.gov/5.19#E4, Release 1.0.6 of 2013-05-06.</ref>
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)}R^n,</math>
where {{math|Γ}} is [[Euler]]'s [[gamma function]].  The gamma function is offset from but  otherwise extends the [[factorial]] function to non-[[integer]] [[argument of a function|arguments]].  It satisfies {{tmath|1= \Gamma(n) = (n-1)!}} if {{math|''n''}} is a positive integer and {{tmath|1= \Gamma\bigl(n + \tfrac12\bigr) = \sqrt{\pi} \cdot \bigl(n - \tfrac12\bigr) \cdot \bigl(n - \tfrac32\bigr) \cdots \tfrac12 }} if {{math|''n''}} is a non-negative integer.

=== Two-dimension recurrence relation ===
The volume can be computed without use of the Gamma function.  As is proved [[Volume of an n-ball#The two-dimension recursion formula|below]] using a vector-calculus [[double integral]] in [[polar coordinates]], the volume {{math|''V''}} of an {{math|''n''}}-ball of radius {{math|''R''}} can be expressed recursively in terms of the volume of an {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}-ball, via the interleaved [[recurrence relation]]:
<math display="block">
V_n(R) = \begin{cases}
1 &\text{if } n=0,\\[0.5ex]
2R &\text{if } n=1,\\[0.5ex]
\dfrac{2\pi}{n}R^2 \times V_{n-2}(R) &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
</math>
This allows computation of {{math|''V''{{sub|''n''}}(''R'')}} in approximately {{math|''n'' / 2}} steps.

=== Alternative forms ===
The volume can also be expressed in terms of an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-ball using the one-dimension recurrence relation:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
V_0(R) &= 1, \\
V_n(R) &= \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + \tfrac12 \bigr)\sqrt\pi}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)}R\, V_{n-1}(R).
\end{align}</math>

Inverting the above, the radius of an {{math|''n''}}-ball of volume {{math|''V''}} can be expressed recursively in terms of the radius of an {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}- or {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-ball:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
R_n(V) &= \bigl(\tfrac12n\bigr)^{1/n}\left(\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr) V\right)^{-2/(n(n-2))}R_{n-2}(V), \\
R_n(V) &= \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)^{1/n}}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + \tfrac12 \bigr)^{1/(n-1)}}V^{-1/(n(n-1))}R_{n-1}(V).
\end{align}</math>

Using explicit formulas for [[particular values of the gamma function]] at the integers and [[half-integer]]s gives formulas for the volume of a Euclidean ball in terms of [[factorial]]s.  For non-negative integer {{mvar|k}}, these are:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
V_{2k}(R) &= \frac{\pi^k}{k!}R^{2k}, \\
V_{2k+1}(R) &= \frac{2(k!)(4\pi)^k}{(2k + 1)!}R^{2k+1}.
\end{align}</math>

The volume can also be expressed in terms of [[double factorial]]s.  For a positive odd integer {{math|2''k'' + 1}}, the double factorial is defined by
<math display="block">(2k + 1)!! = (2k + 1) \cdot (2k - 1) \dotsm 5 \cdot 3 \cdot 1.</math>
The volume of an odd-dimensional ball is
<math display="block">V_{2k+1}(R) = \frac{2(2\pi)^k}{(2k + 1)!!}R^{2k+1}.</math>
There are multiple conventions for double factorials of even integers.  Under the [[Double factorial#Complex arguments|convention]] in which the double factorial satisfies
<math display="block">(2k)!! = (2k) \cdot (2k - 2) \dotsm 4 \cdot 2 \cdot \sqrt{2/\pi} = 2^k \cdot k! \cdot \sqrt{2/\pi},</math>
the volume of an {{math|''n''}}-dimensional ball is, regardless of whether {{math|''n''}} is even or odd,
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{2(2\pi)^{(n-1)/2}}{n!!}R^n.</math>

If the convention <math>(2k)!! = (2k) \cdot (2k - 2) \dotsm 4 \cdot 2</math> for double factorials is used, without the factor of {{tmath|\sqrt{2/\pi} }}, then the volume of an {{math|''n''}}-dimensional ball is, regardless of whether {{math|''n''}} is even or odd,
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{(\pi/2)^{\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor}(2R)^n}{n!!}.</math>

Instead of expressing the volume {{math|''V''}} of the ball in terms of its radius {{math|''R''}}, the formulas can be [[inverse function|inverted]] to express the radius as a function of the volume:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
R_n(V) &= \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)^{1/n}}{\sqrt{\pi}}V^{1/n} \\
&= \left(\frac{n!! V}{2(2\pi)^{(n-1)/2}}\right)^{1/n} \\
R_{2k}(V) &= \frac{(k!V)^{1/(2k)}}{\sqrt{\pi}}, \\
R_{2k+1}(V) &= \left(\frac{(2k+1)!V}{2(k!)(4\pi)^k}\right)^{1/(2k+1)}.\end{align}</math>

=== Approximation for high dimensions===
[[Stirling's approximation]] for the gamma function can be used to approximate the volume when the number of dimensions is high.
<math display="block">V_n(R) \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{n\pi}}\left(\frac{2\pi e}{n}\right)^{n/2}R^n.</math>
<math display="block">R_n(V) \sim (\pi n)^{1/(2n)}\sqrt{\frac{n}{2\pi e}} V^{1/n}.</math>
In particular, for any fixed value of {{math|''R''}} the volume tends to a limiting value of 0 as {{math|''n''}} goes to infinity. Which value of {{mvar|n}} maximizes {{math|''V''{{sub|''n''}}(''R'')}} depends upon the value of {{mvar|R}}; for example, the volume {{math|''V''<sub>''n''</sub>(1)}} is increasing for {{math|0 ≤ ''n'' ≤ 5}}, achieves its maximum when {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}}, and is decreasing for {{math|''n'' ≥ 5}}.<ref>Smith, David J. and Vamanamurthy, Mavina K., "How Small Is a Unit Ball?", Mathematics Magazine, Volume 62, Issue 2, 1989, pp. 101–107, https://doi.org/10.1080/0025570X.1989.11977419.</ref>

Also, there is an asymptotic formula for the surface area<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~songmei/Teaching/STAT260_Spring2021/Lecture_notes/scribe_lecture7.pdf | title=Lecture 7: Concentration Inequalities and Field theoretic calculations | date=2021-02-10 | author=Song Mei | website=www.stat.berkeley.edu}}</ref><math display="block">\lim_n \frac 1n \ln A_{n-1}(\sqrt n) = \frac 12 (\ln(2\pi) + 1)</math>

=== Relation with surface area ===
[[File:Surface areas of unit hyperspheres.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Surface areas of hyperspheres in dimensions 0 through 25]]

Let {{math|''A''{{sub|''n'' − 1}}(''R'')}} denote the hypervolume of the [[n-sphere|{{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-sphere]] of radius {{math|''R''}}. The {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-sphere is the {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-dimensional boundary (surface) of the {{math|''n''}}-dimensional ball of radius {{math|''R''}}, and the sphere's hypervolume and the ball's hypervolume are related by:
<math display="block">A_{n-1}(R) = \frac{d}{dR} V_{n}(R) = \frac{n}{R}V_{n}(R).</math>

Thus, {{math|''A''{{sub|''n'' − 1}}(''R'')}} inherits formulas and recursion relationships from {{math|''V''{{sub|''n''}}(''R'')}}, such as
<math display="block">A_{n-1}(R) = \frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr)}R^{n-1}.</math>
There are also formulas in terms of factorials and double factorials.

== Proofs ==
There are many proofs of the above formulas.

=== The volume is proportional to the {{math|''n''}}th power of the radius ===
An important step in several proofs about volumes of {{math|''n''}}-balls, and a generally useful fact besides, is that the volume of the {{math|''n''}}-ball of radius {{math|''R''}} is proportional to {{math|''R''<sup>''n''</sup>}}:
<math display="block">V_n(R) \propto R^n.</math>
The proportionality constant is the volume of the unit ball.

This is a special case of a general fact about volumes in {{math|''n''}}-dimensional space: If {{math|''K''}}
is a body ([[measurable set]]) in that space and {{math|''RK''}} is the body obtained by stretching in all directions by the factor {{math|''R''}} then the volume of {{math|''RK''}} equals {{math|''R''<sup>''n''</sup>}} times the volume of {{math|''K''}}. This is a direct consequence of the change of variables formula:
<math display="block"> V(RK) = \int_{RK} dx = \int_K R^n\, dy = R^n V(K) </math>
where {{math|1=''dx'' = ''dx''<sub>1</sub>…''dx<sub>n</sub>''}} and the substitution {{math|1=''x'' = ''Ry''}} was made.

Another proof of the above relation, which avoids multi-dimensional [[integral|integration]], uses [[mathematical induction|induction]]: The base case is {{math|''n'' {{=}} 0}}, where the proportionality is obvious. For the inductive step, assume that proportionality is true in dimension {{math|''n'' − 1}}. Note that the intersection of an ''n''-ball with a [[hyperplane]] is an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-ball. When the volume of the {{math|''n''}}-ball is written as the integral of volumes of {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-balls:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \int_{-R}^R V_{n-1}\!\left(\sqrt{R^2 - x^2}\right) dx,</math>
it is possible by the inductive hypothesis to remove a factor of {{math|''R''}} from the radius of the {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-ball to get:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = R^{n-1}\! \int_{-R}^R V_{n-1}\!\left(\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{x}{R}\right)^2}\right) dx.</math>
Making the change of variables {{math|''t'' {{=}} ''{{sfrac|x|R}}''}} leads to:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = R^n\! \int_{-1}^1 V_{n-1}\!\left(\sqrt{1 - t^2}\right) dt = R^n V_n(1),</math>
which demonstrates the proportionality relation in dimension {{math|''n''}}. By induction, the proportionality relation is true in all dimensions.

=== The two-dimension recursion formula ===
A proof of the recursion formula relating the volume of the {{math|''n''}}-ball and an {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}-ball can be given using the proportionality formula above and integration in [[Cylindrical coordinate system|cylindrical coordinates]]. Fix a plane through the center of the ball. Let {{math|''r''}} denote the distance between a point in the plane and the center of the sphere, and let {{math|''θ''}} denote the azimuth. Intersecting the {{math|''n''}}-ball with the {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}-dimensional plane defined by fixing a radius and an azimuth gives an {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}-ball of radius {{tmath|\textstyle \sqrt{R^2 - r^2} }}. The volume of the ball can therefore be written as an iterated integral of the volumes of the {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}-balls over the possible radii and azimuths:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^R V_{n-2}\!\left(\sqrt{R^2 - r^2}\right) r\,dr\,d\theta,</math>
The azimuthal coordinate can be immediately integrated out. Applying the proportionality relation shows that the volume equals
<math display="block">V_n(R) = 2\pi V_{n-2}(R) \int_0^R \left(1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right)^{(n-2)/2}\,r\,dr.</math>
The integral can be evaluated by making the substitution {{math|''u'' {{=}} 1 − (''{{sfrac|r|R}}''){{su|p=2}}}} to get
<math display="block">\begin{align}
V_n(R) &= 2\pi V_{n-2}(R) \cdot \left[-\frac{R^2}{n}\left(1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right)^{n/2}\right]_{r=0}^{r=R} \\
&= \frac{2\pi R^2}{n} V_{n-2}(R),
\end{align}</math>
which is the two-dimension recursion formula.

The same technique can be used to give an inductive proof of the volume formula. The base cases of the induction are the 0-ball and the 1-ball, which can be checked directly using the facts {{tmath|1= \Gamma(1) = 1}} and {{tmath|1= \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr) = \tfrac12 \cdot \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr) = \tfrac\pi2}}. The inductive step is similar to the above, but instead of applying proportionality to the volumes of the {{math|(''n'' − 2)}}-balls, the inductive hypothesis is applied instead.

=== The one-dimension recursion formula ===
The proportionality relation can also be used to prove the recursion formula relating the volumes of an {{math|''n''}}-ball and an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-ball. As in the proof of the proportionality formula, the volume of an {{math|''n''}}-ball can be written as an integral over the volumes of {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-balls. Instead of making a substitution, however, the proportionality relation can be applied to the volumes of the {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-balls in the [[integrand]]:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = V_{n-1}(R) \int_{-R}^R \left(1 - \left(\frac{x}{R}\right)^2\right)^{(n-1)/2} \,dx.</math>
The integrand is an [[even function]], so by symmetry the interval of integration can be restricted to {{math|[0, ''R'']}}. On the interval {{math|[0, ''R'']}}, it is possible to apply the substitution {{math|''u'' {{=}} (''{{sfrac|x|R}}''){{su|p=2}}}}. This transforms the expression into
<math display="block">V_{n-1}(R) \cdot R \cdot \int_0^1 (1-u)^{(n-1)/2}u^{-\frac12}\,du</math>
The integral is a value of a well-known [[special function]] called the [[beta function]] {{math|Β(''x'', ''y'')}}, and the volume in terms of the beta function is
<math display="block">V_n(R) = V_{n-1}(R) \cdot R \cdot \Beta\left(\tfrac{n + 1}2, \tfrac12\right).</math>
The beta function can be expressed in terms of the gamma function in much the same way that factorials are related to [[binomial coefficient]]s. Applying this relationship gives
<math display="block">V_n(R) = V_{n-1}(R) \cdot R \cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + \tfrac12 \bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)}.</math>
Using the value {{tmath|1= \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr) = \sqrt{\pi} }} gives the one-dimension recursion formula:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = R\sqrt{\pi}\frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + \tfrac12\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)} V_{n-1}(R).</math>

As with the two-dimension recursive formula, the same technique can be used to give an inductive proof of the volume formula.

=== Direct integration in spherical coordinates ===
The volume of the ''n''-ball <math>V_n(R)</math> can be computed by integrating the [[volume element]] in [[N-sphere#Spherical coordinates|spherical coordinates]]. The [[spherical coordinate system]] has a radial coordinate {{math|''r''}} and angular coordinates {{math|''φ''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''φ''<sub>''n'' − 1</sub>}}, where the domain of each {{math|''φ''}} except {{math|''φ''<sub>''n'' − 1</sub>}} is {{math|[0, {{pi}})}}, and the domain of {{math|''φ''<sub>''n'' − 1</sub>}} is {{math|[0, 2{{pi}})}}. The spherical volume element is:
<math display="block">dV = r^{n-1}\sin^{n-2}(\varphi_1)\sin^{n-3}(\varphi_2) \cdots \sin(\varphi_{n-2})\,dr\,d\varphi_1\,d\varphi_2 \cdots d\varphi_{n-1},</math>
and the volume is the integral of this quantity over {{math|''r''}} between 0 and {{math|''R''}} and all possible angles:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \int_0^R \int_0^\pi \cdots \int_0^{2\pi} r^{n-1}\sin^{n-2}(\varphi_1) \cdots \sin(\varphi_{n-2})\,d\varphi_{n-1} \cdots d\varphi_1\,dr.</math>
Each of the factors in the integrand depends on only a single variable, and therefore the iterated integral can be written as a product of integrals:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \left(\int_0^R r^{n-1}\,dr\right)\!\left(\int_0^\pi \sin^{n-2}(\varphi_1)\,d\varphi_1\right)\cdots\left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\varphi_{n-1}\right).</math>
The integral over the radius is {{math|''{{sfrac|R<sup>n</sup>|n}}''}}. The intervals of integration on the angular coordinates can, by the symmetry of the sine about {{sfrac|{{pi}}|2}}, be changed to {{math|[0, {{sfrac|{{pi}}|2}}]}}:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{R^n}{n} \left(2\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^{n-2}(\varphi_1)\,d\varphi_1\right) \cdots \left(4\int_0^{\pi/2} d\varphi_{n-1}\right).</math>
Each of the remaining integrals is now a particular value of the beta function:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{R^n}{n} \Beta\bigl(\tfrac{n-1}2, \tfrac12\bigr) \Beta\bigl(\tfrac{n-2}2, \tfrac12\bigr) \cdots \Beta\bigl(1, \tfrac12\bigr) \cdot 2\,\Beta\bigl(\tfrac12, \tfrac12\bigr).</math>

The beta functions can be rewritten in terms of gamma functions:

<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{R^n}{n} \cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 - \tfrac12\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 - 1\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 - \tfrac12\bigr)} \cdots \frac{\Gamma(1)\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)} \cdot 2 \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)}{\Gamma(1)}.</math>

This product telescopes. Combining this with the values {{tmath|1= \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr) = \sqrt{\pi} }} and {{tmath|1= \Gamma(1) = 1}} and the functional equation {{tmath|1= z\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z+1)}} leads to

<math display="block">V_n(R) = \frac{2\pi^{n/2}R^n}{n\,\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr)} = \frac{\pi^{n/2}R^n}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)}.</math>

=== Gaussian integrals ===
The volume formula can be proven directly using [[Gaussian integral]]s. Consider the function:
<math display="block">f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = {\exp}\biggl({-\tfrac12 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}\biggr).</math>
This function is both rotationally invariant and a product of functions of one variable each. Using the fact that it is a product and the formula for the Gaussian integral gives:
<math display="block">\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} f \,dV = \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp\left(-\tfrac12 x_i^2\right)\,dx_i\right) = (2\pi)^{n/2},</math>
where {{math|''dV''}} is the {{math|''n''}}-dimensional volume element. Using [[rotational invariance]], the same integral can be computed in spherical coordinates:
<math display="block">\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} f \,dV = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}(r)} \exp\left(-\tfrac12 r^2\right) \,dA\,dr,</math>
where {{math|''S''<sup>''n'' − 1</sup>(''r'')}} is an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-sphere of radius {{math|''r''}} (being the surface of an {{math|''n''}}-ball of radius {{math|''r''}}) and {{math|''dA''}} is the area element (equivalently, the {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-dimensional volume element). The surface area of the sphere satisfies a proportionality equation similar to the one for the volume of a ball: If {{math|''A''<sub>''n'' − 1</sub>(''r'')}} is the surface area of an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-sphere of radius {{math|''r''}}, then:
<math display="block">A_{n-1}(r) = r^{n-1} A_{n-1}(1).</math>
Applying this to the above integral gives the expression
<math display="block">(2\pi)^{n/2} = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}(r)} \exp\left(-\tfrac12 r^2\right) \,dA\,dr  =  A_{n-1}(1) \int_0^\infty \exp\left(-\tfrac12 r^2\right)\,r^{n-1}\,dr.</math>
Substituting {{math|''t'' {{=}} {{sfrac|''r''<sup>2</sup>|2}}}}:
<math display="block">\int_0^\infty \exp\left(-\tfrac12 r^2\right)\,r^{n-1}\,dr  =  2^{(n-2)/2} \int_0^\infty e^{-t} t^{(n-2)/2}\,dt.</math>
The integral on the right is the gamma function evaluated at {{math|{{sfrac|''n''|2}}}}.

Combining the two results shows that
<math display="block">A_{n-1}(1) = \frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr)}.</math>
To derive the volume of an {{math|''n''}}-ball of radius {{math|''R''}} from this formula, integrate the surface area of a sphere of radius {{math|''r''}} for {{math|0 ≤ ''r'' ≤ ''R''}} and apply the functional equation {{math|''z''Γ(''z'') {{=}} Γ(''z'' + 1)}}:
<math display="block">V_n(R) = \int_0^R \frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr)} \,r^{n-1}\,dr = \frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{n\,\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2\bigr)}R^n = \frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac n2 + 1\bigr)}R^n.</math>

=== Geometric proof ===

The relations {{tmath|1= V_{n+1}(R) = \tfrac{R}{n+1}A_n(R)}} and {{tmath|1= A_{n+1}(R) = (2\pi R)V_n(R)}} and thus the volumes of {{mvar|n}}-balls and areas of {{mvar|n}}-spheres can also be derived geometrically.  As noted above, because a ball of radius {{tmath|R}} is obtained from a unit ball {{tmath|B_n}} by rescaling all directions in {{tmath|R}} times, {{tmath|V_n(R)}} is proportional to {{tmath|\textstyle R^n}}, which implies that {{tmath|1= \tfrac{d}{dR}V_n(R) = \tfrac{n}{R} V_n(R)}}.  Also, {{tmath|1= A_{n-1}(R) = \tfrac{d}{dR}V_n(R)}}, since a ball is a union of [[concentric spheres]] and increasing the radius by {{mvar|ε}} sweeps out a shell of thickness {{mvar|ε}}.  Thus, {{tmath|1= V_{n}(R) = \tfrac{R}{n}A_{n-1}(R)}}.

Furthermore, {{tmath|1= A_{n+1}(R) = (2\pi R)V_n(R)}}, since a volume-preserving [[bijection]] between the unit sphere ({{tmath|S_{n+1} }}) and {{tmath|S_1 \times B_n}} exists:
<math display="block">(x,y,\vec{z}) \mapsto \left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}},\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}},\vec{z}\right)</math>
({{tmath|\vec{z} }} is an {{mvar|n}}-[[tuple]]; {{tmath|1=\vert (x,y,\vec{z})\vert =1}}; we are ignoring sets of measure 0).  Volume is preserved because at each point; the difference from [[isometry]] is a stretching in the ''xy'' plane (by <math display="inline">1/\!\sqrt{x^2+y^2}</math> times in the direction of constant {{tmath|\textstyle x^2+y^2}}) that exactly matches the compression in the direction of the [[gradient]] of <math>|\vec{z}|</math> on {{tmath|S_n}} (with the relevant angles being equal).  For {{tmath|S_2}}, a similar argument was originally made by [[Archimedes]] in ''[[On the Sphere and Cylinder]]''.

== Balls in {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} norms ==
There are also explicit expressions for the volumes of balls in [[Lp space|{{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} norm]]s. The {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} norm of the vector {{math|''x'' {{=}} (''x''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''x''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is
<math display="block">\|x\|_p = \biggl(\sum_{i=1}^n | x_i |^p \biggr)^{\! 1/p},</math>
and an {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} ball is the set of all vectors whose {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} norm is less than or equal to a fixed number called the radius of the ball. The case {{math|''p'' {{=}} 2}} is the standard [[Euclidean distance]] function, but other values of {{math|''p''}} occur in diverse contexts such as [[information theory]], [[coding theory]], and [[dimensional regularization]].

The volume of an {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} ball of radius {{math|''R''}} is

<math display="block">V^p_n(R) = \frac{\Bigl(2\,\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1p + 1\bigr)\Bigr)^n}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac np + 1\bigr)}R^n.</math>

These volumes satisfy recurrence relations similar to those for {{math|''p'' {{=}} 2}}:

<math display="block">V^p_n(R) = \frac{\Bigl(2\,\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1p + 1\bigr)\Bigr)^p p}{n} R^p \, V^p_{n-p}(R)</math>

and 

<math display="block">V^p_n(R) = 2 \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1p + 1\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac{n-1}p + 1\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac np + 1\bigr)} R \, V^p_{n-1}(R),</math>

which can be written more concisely using a [[Binomial coefficient#Two_real_or_complex_valued_arguments|generalized binomial coefficient]],

<math display="block">V^p_n(R) =  \frac{2}{\dbinom{n/p}{1/p}} R \, V^p_{n-1}(R).</math>

For {{math|''p'' {{=}} 2}}, one recovers the recurrence for the volume of a Euclidean ball because {{math|2Γ({{sfrac|3|2}}) {{=}} {{radic|{{pi}}}}}}.

For example, in the cases {{math|''p'' {{=}} 1}} ([[taxicab norm]]) and {{math|''p'' {{=}} ∞}} ([[max norm]]), the volumes are:
<math display="block">\begin{align} V^1_n(R) &= \frac{2^n}{n!}R^n, \\ V^\infty_n(R) &= 2^n R^n. \end{align}</math>
These agree with elementary calculations of the volumes of [[cross-polytope]]s and [[hypercube]]s.

=== Relation with surface area ===
For most values of {{math|''p''}}, the surface area <math>A_{n-1}^p(R)</math> of an {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} sphere of radius {{math|''R''}} (the boundary of an {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} {{math|''n''}}-ball of radius {{math|''R''}}) cannot be calculated by [[derivative|differentiating]] the volume of an {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} ball with respect to its radius. While the volume can be expressed as an integral over the surface areas using the [[coarea formula]], the coarea formula contains a correction factor that accounts for how the {{math|''p''}}-norm varies from point to point. For {{math|''p'' {{=}} 2}} and {{math|''p'' {{=}} ∞}}, this factor is one. However, if {{math|''p'' {{=}} 1}} then the correction factor is {{tmath|\sqrt{n} }}}: the surface area of an {{math|''L''<sup>1</sup>}} sphere of radius {{math|''R''}} in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is {{tmath|\sqrt{n} }} times the derivative of the volume of an {{math|''L''<sup>1</sup>}} ball.  This can be seen most simply by applying the [[divergence theorem]] to the [[vector field]] {{math|'''F'''(x) {{=}} x}} to get

{{bi|left=1.6|1= {{nobr|1= <math>nV^1_n(R) = </math>{{oiint
| preintegral = <math>\iiint_V\left(\mathbf{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf{F}\right)\,dV=</math>
| intsubscpt = <math>\scriptstyle S</math>
| integrand = <math>(\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n})\,dS </math>
}} {{br}} <math>\phantom{nV^1_n(R)}\vphantom{\Biggl(} = </math> {{oiint
| intsubscpt = <math>\scriptstyle S</math>
| integrand = <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(\vert x_1\vert +\cdots+\vert x_n\vert )\,dS </math>
}}  <math> = \frac{R}{\sqrt{n}} </math>{{oiint
| intsubscpt = <math>\scriptstyle S</math>
| integrand = <math>\,dS </math>
}} {{br}} <math>\phantom{nV^1_n(R)}\vphantom{\Biggl(} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{n}} A^1_{n-1}(R).</math>}} }}
For other values of {{math|''p''}}, the constant is a complicated integral.

=== Generalizations ===
The volume formula can be generalized even further. For [[positive real numbers]] {{math|''p''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''p''<sub>''n''</sub>}}, define the {{math|(''p''<sub>1</sub>, …, ''p''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} ball with limit {{math|''L'' ≥ 0}} to be
<math display="block">B_{p_1, \ldots, p_n}(L) = \left\{ x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathbf{R}^n : \vert x_1 \vert^{p_1} + \cdots + \vert x_n \vert^{p_n} \le L \right\}.</math>
The volume of this ball has been known since the time of Dirichlet:<ref>{{cite journal|last=Dirichlet|first=P. G. Lejeune|title=Sur une nouvelle méthode pour la détermination des intégrales multiples|trans-title=On a novel method for determining multiple integrals|journal=Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées|volume=4|date=1839|pages=164–168}}</ref>
<math display="block">V\bigl(B_{p_1, \ldots, p_n}(L)\bigr) = \frac{2^n \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1{p_1} + 1\bigr) \cdots \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1{p_n} + 1\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1{p_1} + \cdots + \tfrac1{p_n} + 1\bigr)} L^{\tfrac1{p_1} + \cdots + \tfrac1{p_n}}.</math>

==== Comparison to {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} norm ====
Using the [[harmonic mean]] <math>p = \frac{n}{\frac{1}{p_1} + \cdots \frac{1}{p_n}}</math> and defining <math>R = \sqrt[p]{L}</math>, the similarity to the volume formula for the {{math|''L''{{isup|''p''}}}} ball becomes clear.
<math display="block">V\left(\left\{ x \in \mathbf{R}^n : \sqrt[p]{\vert x_1 \vert^{p_1} + \cdots + \vert x_n \vert^{p_n}} \le R \right\}\right) = \frac{2^n \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1{p_1} + 1\bigr) \cdots \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac1{p_n} + 1\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac{n}{p} + 1\bigr)} R^n.</math>
